analysis: Examined the two head_text excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (lines 15179-17216). They contain only test fixture data: gemma-4-26b and gemma-4-26b-8bit chat/completion cases with request_body, provider_body, template_input, plan (prompt_contract_id, block_boundaries, chain_hash) and token_ids. The same prompt_contract_id (7fa068ec...) appears throughout. The patch excerpt shows the changed fixture content (an additional_context enable_thinking field, changed token counts and chain hashes in another model's block, and a few other range shifts). I found no secrets, credentials, keys, executable code, endpoint or authorization logic, or change to any trust boundary (TB-002, TB-011) or asset (A-001, A-003, A-016). The fixtures include synthetic tool-call and harmony-framing strings, such as a write_file tool call to /tmp/report.txt and an assistant-role message containing <|channel|> markers. These are test inputs for prompt-template rendering parity, and the supplied evidence does not show that any production code path changes. The fixtures cover cache-routing inputs (block_boundaries chain hashes, cache_routing_eligible), which relate to the T-041 prefix-cache sharing and timing oracle. Regenerated hashes and token IDs affect only cache key derivation parity between the coordinator and the provider. The security consequence would depend on the unseen consuming code, which was not supplied. The patch excerpt is truncated, and the paired Go/Swift generators and consumers were not supplied, so whether fixtures and implementations agree cannot be confirmed from this batch. Correct parity is a correctness and availability concern (cache misses or mismatched routing), not a demonstrated vulnerability. No finding qualifies.
